newsitem.title: UK: EMU tussle favours dollar, sterling, yen - for now.
newsitem.headline: EMU tussle favours dollar, sterling, yen - for now.

text.p: Traders torn between betting on a broad European economic and monetary union (EMU) and a delay in its launch are sitting on the fence by buying dollars, sterling, yen and market volatility, analysts said on Monday.
The victory for the left in French elections on Sunday is seen boosting the chances that Italy and Spain will be among the founder members of EMU, they said.
A row between the German government and the Bundesbank about plans to revalue the central bank's assets has also fanned talk of a broad EMU.
This has undermined the mark against other major currencies and driven it back from its highs against other European units.
Traders are not convinced that EMU will start on time in 1999, though, and are wary that Germany would prefer to delay EMU rather than replace the mark with a potentially softer and weaker currency.
"You can have a weak euro now or a hard euro later but you can't have a hard euro now," said Nigel Morgan, economic strategist at Old Mutual Portfolio Managers.
"People don't know how all this is going to play out so they're saying give me dollars, sterling, yen, Swiss francs -- anything which isn't involved in EMU," he said.
"We have built up our holding of very short yen paper, which is basically a bet the yen will rise."
The mark has already hit a three-week low against the pound and the dollar and weakened to a one-week low against the yen.
Concern about the outlook for EMU has also boosted volatility on European cross rates in the past week.

One-month mark/Paris implied volatility is up at 3.20/70 percent from 1.70/2.0 before the first round of the French elections were held on May 25. One-month mark/lira volatility is 6.50/7.50 from 3.50/4.00 a week ago.
Traders looking for a summer of volatility and one-way bets may be disappointed, though, analysts said.
"The market has got its fingers badly burnt by shorting the franc in the past and will do it again this time," said Peter von Maydell, currency strategist at UBS.
"It's lost sight of the plot, which is that underlying everything is the policy of currency convergence."
Bank of France intervention to prevent the franc falling too far from its central Exchange Rate Mechanism parity of 3.35386 per mark will keep volatility in check, analysts said.
"I think there will be high volumes in mark/Paris but not necessarily high volatility," said Robert Prior-Wandesforde, an economist at HSBC Markets.
"If there is any pressure on the franc, and a danger of a move to 3.39 or 3.40, we will see intervention straight away."
The mark has kept within one percent of its central ERM parity rate against the franc so far this year, despite a decline to 3.3860 per mark on Monday, its weakest since December 11, 1995.
With domestic investors holding nearly 90 percent of French notes and bonds, there is limited scope for a large-scale run on the franc, analysts said.
"We're not looking for a collapse within Europe," said Morgan at Old Mutual.

Meanwhile, the extent to which the dollar can benefit from tensions over EMU will be limited by the knowledge that Japan, and possibly the United States, will speak out if dollar gains against the mark drag the U.S. currency up too far against the yen.
Demand for dollars will also be dampened if the premium U.S. notes offer over their German counterparts falls much further, said von Maydell at UBS.
"The dollar is a sell as there is no logical reason for it to be rising when the yield spread between the T-notes and the bunds has fallen so much," he said.
The spread between the 10-year benchmark Bund and T-note has fallen to 82 basis points from 87 basis points on Friday.
